title: Lagrange and Hamilton, continuum and tensors, finite elements, control, computation, visual libraries, exercises

chapters.title: Hamiltonian mechanics
chapters.what: Trade velocities for momenta: H(q, p) = T + V, and the state moves through phase space by q̇ = ∂H/∂p, ṗ = −∂H/∂q. Orbits follow level curves of H, and phase-space area is conserved (Liouville).
maths: \dot q=\dfrac{\partial H}{\partial p},\qquad \dot p=-\dfrac{\partial H}{\partial q}
chapters.looks: Phase portraits: level curves of H, the separatrix, the orbit and a blob of neighbouring states (2D); the surface H(q, p) with the orbit riding on it (3D).
chapters.change: Switch the integrator: symplectic methods keep the orbit on its level curve; explicit Euler spirals outwards.
chapters.use: Celestial mechanics, accelerator beam optics, molecular dynamics, statistical mechanics.
misc: Phase space is not physical space.
A symplectic integrator does not conserve energy exactly, but its error stays bounded.

examples.title: The pendulum's phase portrait
examples.world: Closed curves inside the separatrix are swings; the leapfrog period matches the exact elliptic-integral value.

examples.title: Over the top: outside the separatrix

examples.title: Liouville: phase-space area is conserved

examples.title: Explicit Euler inflates phase space
examples.world: Each Euler step multiplies areas by 1 + h²ω²: after 400 steps the blob is 2.71× larger.

examples.title: Symplectic integrators for planets
examples.world: Leapfrog keeps a Kepler orbit's period right over many revolutions (Ruth 1983; Verlet 1967).

examples.title: A double well and its separatrix
examples.world: Ammonia inversion and bistable switches: two wells separated by a figure-eight separatrix.

examples.title: Noether: symmetry means conservation
examples.world: No explicit time dependence in H → energy is conserved; a rotation symmetry → angular momentum.

chapters.title: Continuum description
chapters.what: A continuum is followed either by particle labels X (material, Lagrangian) or by fixed points x (spatial, Eulerian). The motion x = φ(X, t) stretches and rotates material; its gradient F = ∂x/∂X measures the local deformation, and J = det F the volume change.
maths: \mathbf x=\varphi(\mathbf X,t),\quad \mathbf F=\dfrac{\partial\mathbf x}{\partial\mathbf X},\ J=\det\mathbf F
chapters.looks: A material grid carried and distorted by the velocity field, with a small square mapped by F (2D); particle paths in (x, y, t) (3D).
chapters.change: Play the motion: the square shears, rotates or stretches; J stays 1 for incompressible flows.
chapters.use: Metal forming, polymer processing, blood flow, glaciers, crash simulation.
misc: Material and spatial descriptions give the same physics.
A steady flow can still accelerate particles (convective acceleration).

examples.title: Simple shear: the deformation gradient
examples.world: A rubber mount or a sheared deck of cards: F = [[1, γ], [0, 1]] with γ = aT.

examples.title: Rigid rotation: F is a rotation
examples.world: A quarter turn: F = [[0, −1], [1, 0]] and J = 1.

examples.title: Pure shear: stretch without volume change
examples.world: Extensional flow in fibre spinning: F = diag(e^{aT}, e^{−aT}).

examples.title: A Rankine vortex: rotating core
examples.world: Tornadoes and bathtub vortices: the core turns like a solid body, vorticity 2a/r_c = 4.

examples.title: …and irrotational outside
examples.world: Outside the core the fluid circulates without spinning: vorticity 0.

examples.title: Material derivative in a steady flow
examples.world: In a steady converging flow particles still accelerate: |(u·∇)u| = ½√(e + e⁻¹) here.

chapters.title: Conservation laws
chapters.what: Mass, momentum, angular momentum and energy are conserved for any piece of material. In a continuum each law becomes a balance: rate of change inside = flux in − flux out + sources.
chapters.looks: Each balance applied to a concrete system (2D); the matching 3D picture (3D).
chapters.change: Change a parameter and watch the conserved quantity stay fixed while the others adjust.
chapters.use: Every simulation code: CFD, crash, weather, combustion.
misc: Conservation of momentum does not mean conservation of kinetic energy.
Symmetry of the stress tensor is angular-momentum balance.

examples.title: Mass: density falls as material expands
examples.world: A gas expanding uniformly: ρ/ρ₀ = 1/J = e^{−2aT}.

examples.title: Continuity in a pipe contraction
examples.world: Halve the diameter and the speed quadruples (Venturi meters, garden-hose nozzles).

examples.title: Momentum: a head-on elastic collision
examples.world: Newton's cradle: equal masses swap velocities.

examples.title: Angular momentum: Kepler's second law
examples.world: Conserved L reduces the orbit to a 1D radial problem with period 2πa^{3/2}.

examples.title: Energy: a car on a roller-coaster
examples.world: Potential and kinetic energy trade; the total stays fixed without friction.

examples.title: An incompressible Taylor–Green flow
examples.world: A divergence-free field conserves area: the textbook test case for CFD codes.

chapters.title: Tensor calculus for mechanics
chapters.what: A second-order tensor maps vectors to vectors (a plane's normal to its traction). Its components change when the axes rotate, T′ = QᵀTQ, but its invariants (trace, determinant, principal values) do not.
maths: I_1=\operatorname{tr}\mathbf T,\ I_2=\tfrac12[(\operatorname{tr}\mathbf T)^2-\operatorname{tr}\mathbf T^2],\ I_3=\det\mathbf T
chapters.looks: Components T′₁₁, T′₂₂, T′₁₂ as the axes rotate, crossing the principal values (2D); the stress ellipsoid, principal axes, rotated frame and traction on a plane (3D).
chapters.change: Rotate the axes: every component changes, the principal values and invariants never do.
chapters.use: Stress analysis, strain gauges, anisotropic materials, inertia tensors, diffusion MRI.
misc: A tensor is not just a matrix: the matrix is its components in one basis.
Principal stresses are the extreme normal stresses; shear vanishes on principal planes.

examples.title: Principal stresses
examples.world: A loaded shaft's stress state: rotate until the shear vanishes.

examples.title: Transforming components
examples.world: Rotating the axes by 30° gives the normal stress read by a strain-gauge rosette arm.

examples.title: The trace is invariant
examples.world: About any axis, tr T′ = tr T = 90: the mean stress drives volume change.

examples.title: Pure shear and von Mises
examples.world: A shaft in torsion yields when τ = σ_y/√3.

examples.title: Hydrostatic pressure has no shear
examples.world: Deep-sea pressure squeezes a submarine hull equally in every direction: zero shear on every plane.

examples.title: Uniaxial tension: maximum shear at 45°
examples.world: Lüders bands in mild steel form at 45° to the pull, where τ = σ/2.

examples.title: The velocity gradient: stretching plus spin
examples.world: In simple shear flow ∇u splits into a symmetric stretching part and a skew spin of magnitude ½.

chapters.title: FEM foundations
chapters.what: The finite element method splits a domain into elements, approximates the unknown by simple shape functions on each, and asks the weak form to hold for every shape function (Galerkin). Element matrices are assembled into one sparse system K u = f.
chapters.looks: Hat and quadratic shape functions, the FEM solution against the exact one (2D); the assembled stiffness matrix as a bar chart, showing its band (3D).
chapters.change: Add elements or raise the order: the approximation tightens; the matrix stays banded.
chapters.use: Aircraft, bridges, engines, implants, electronics: almost every engineering simulation.
misc: The FEM does not solve the differential equation pointwise; it solves the weak form.
More elements is not the only way to accuracy: higher-order elements converge faster.

examples.title: Hat functions
examples.world: Linear elements interpolate between nodes with 'hat' shape functions.

examples.title: Quadratic shape functions
examples.world: Three-node elements add a mid-side node and curved shape functions.

examples.title: Galerkin's method
examples.world: Courant (1943) proposed piecewise-linear trial functions; in 1D the nodal values come out exact.

examples.title: Assembly gives a banded matrix
examples.world: Turner et al. (1956) assembled element stiffnesses for aircraft wings; each node talks only to its neighbours.

examples.title: Boundary conditions
examples.world: Fix both ends and the mid-span displacement of a uniformly loaded bar is qL²/8EA.

chapters.title: 1D finite elements
chapters.what: A bar element has stiffness (EA/h)[[1, −1], [−1, 1]]. Assembling n of them and applying the supports gives the nodal displacements; stresses follow from the element strains.
chapters.looks: Displacement and axial force, FEM against exact (2D); the stiffness matrix (3D).
chapters.change: Halve the element size: the error between nodes drops four times.
chapters.use: Bolts, cables, piles, truss members, heat conduction in rods (the same equation).
misc: Linear elements give a piecewise-constant stress even when the exact stress varies.
Nodal exactness in 1D is special; it does not carry over to 2D.

examples.title: A steel bolt under a 10 kN pull
examples.world: A 2 m bolt with EA = 2 × 10⁷ N stretches PL/EA = 1 mm.

examples.title: A hanging steel rod under its own weight
examples.world: A 100 m steel rod (A = 1 cm²) in a mine shaft stretches qL²/2EA = 1.93 mm.

examples.title: Interpolation error between nodes: h²/8
examples.world: Nodes are exact but the straight lines between them miss the parabola by h²/8.

examples.title: Halve h, quarter the error
examples.world: Eight elements: the error falls to 1/512.

examples.title: Quadratic elements are exact here
examples.world: A uniform load gives a quadratic u, which two quadratic elements reproduce exactly.

examples.title: A varying load: skin friction on a pile
examples.world: Soil friction varying along a pile: linear elements approximate the curved displacement.

chapters.title: 2D finite elements
chapters.what: In 2D the domain is meshed into triangles or quadrilaterals. A linear triangle has constant gradients; assembling them solves heat conduction, torsion (Prandtl stress function) or plane-stress elasticity.
chapters.looks: The mesh coloured by the solution or von Mises stress, with the deformed shape (2D); the solution as a faceted surface (3D).
chapters.change: Refine the mesh: torsion constant and tip deflection creep up to the exact values (linear triangles are too stiff).
chapters.use: Structural analysis, heat sinks, shafts, dams, electrostatics, ground-water flow.
misc: Constant-strain triangles are too stiff in bending; they converge, but slowly.
A re-entrant corner concentrates error and stress: refine there.

examples.world: Prandtl's stress function on 16 × 16 triangles: J slightly below the exact 0.1406.

chapters.title: Computational workflow
chapters.what: Every simulation states its assumptions, equations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, then a discretisation and solver. It must be verified (does it solve the equations right?) and validated (are they the right equations?), with convergence and error shown.
chapters.looks: A numerical experiment with its error or stability indicator (2D); the matching 3D view (3D).
chapters.change: Change the step size: watch convergence, and the cliff where a method becomes unstable.
chapters.use: Every engineering code, from spreadsheets to supercomputers.
misc: A smooth-looking result can still be wrong: always check convergence.
Round-off error grows as the step shrinks.

examples.title: Explicit Euler goes unstable
examples.world: Stiff systems (chemistry, circuits) blow up when |1 + hλ| > 1.

examples.title: Truncation against round-off
examples.world: Numerical derivatives: too large an h has truncation error, too small has round-off.

examples.title: Convergence at the expected rate

chapters.title: Simulation architecture
chapters.what: A simulation has a scene (geometry, coordinates, boundaries), physics (equations, materials, forces, constraints), controls (sliders, toggles, time) and outputs (animation, graphs, fields, tables). Game engines organise the same parts around a fixed time-step loop.
chapters.looks: Each example is a small simulation with scene, physics, controls and outputs (2D and 3D).
chapters.change: Use the parameter panel (controls) and ▶ (time) and read the outputs table.
chapters.use: Games, digital twins, training simulators, engineering design tools.
misc: The rendering frame rate and the physics step are different things.
Outputs must be computed from the state, not drawn by hand.

examples.world: Scene: ground and ball; physics: gravity (and drag); controls: speed and angle; outputs: range, height, time.
